claims.text: Prolonged exposure to 600–800°C under applied stress induces stress-assisted diffusion in a nominally single-phase HEA.
Stress-assisted diffusion promotes nanoscale solute clustering or ordered nanodomain formation within the grains.
The intragranular clusters locally modify the lattice.
The clusters create preferential sites for crack initiation.
Cluster-induced impediment of dislocation motion causes strain localization.
Strain localization caused by nanoscale clustering reduces toughness and leads to brittle failure.
Embrittlement in conventional alloys is primarily driven by grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering can produce a uniform, fine-grained, nominally single-phase HEA with an equiatomic or near-equiatomic distribution of principal elements.
Combined thermal exposure and applied stress will reduce HEA toughness relative to the as-processed homogeneous state.
Samples aged under applied load will exhibit lower critical stress-intensity factors than samples aged thermally without applied stress.
Samples aged under applied load will initiate cracks earlier than samples aged thermally without applied stress.
The as-processed single-phase HEA has a homogeneous composition and microstructure with high toughness.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply under sustained 600–800°C exposure with concurrent mechanical loading.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures, for short exposures, or without significant mechanical stress.
The exact kinetics of solute clustering and the cluster threshold for initiating brittleness are unknown.
The magnitude by which applied stress accelerates clustering relative to thermal aging alone is uncertain.
